attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: image set up, array set up, game set up, function set up, game events.


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare 2 new arrays and type the image variable names in one, and numbers inside the other?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What images might you use to be collected by the Player sprite in the project?

❓ What symbols should be used to contain and separate the elements in an array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that elements in an array should be contained by a pair of brackets and each element should be separated by a comma.

💡 In the project, different levels will be created where 1 image from the enemyList array will be used as the Enemy sprite and the background color will be set to 1 value from the backgroundColor array. Prompt the ninja to make sure each image can be easily seen in front of the background color it will be paired with.
steps.instructions:
Store image variables and background colors in arrays to use in the project!


Create 4 variables below // image set up and assign them an img`` value. Select 4 different images from the gallery or My Assets, which will be collected by the Player sprite during the project. Update the variable names accordingly. 


Underneath // array set up, use the keyword let to declare a new array called enemyList. Type an assignment operator and a pair of brackets [ ] with the names of the image variables typed inside, separated by commas. 


Create a second array called backgroundColor underneath enemyList. Inside the array’s brackets, type 4 different numbers between 1-15 to use as background colors in the project. 


Now, elements are stored in the enemyList and backgroundColor arrays to be used in the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the shift function to remove the first element from the backgroundColor and enemyList arrays?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the pop function different from the shift function? Why might you use each one?

❓ What will the first background color be set to? What will the first enemy image be set to?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The pop function removes and returns the last element in an array. The shift function removes and returns the first element in an array. The ninja may use either function to get and remove elements from different index values.

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice that the background color will be set to the first element in the backgroundColor array and the enemy’s image will be set to the first element in the enemyList array. As needed, they can rearrange the order of elements in both arrays so that the sprite images are visible against the matching background color.
steps.instructions:
Use elements from the 2 arrays to set the background color and Enemy sprite image!


Open Scene and drag [set background color to (color)] underneath // function set up. Inside the parentheses,  delete 0 then type backgroundColor and a dot operator. Select the shift function from the code completion tool, then type a pair of parentheses. The shift function removes and returns the first element from an array. Now, the first element from backgroundColor will be used in the code and removed from the array.


Below the setBackgroundColor code, use the keyword let to declare a new variable called enemyImage. To the right of the assignment operator, type enemyList and a dot operator. Select the shift function from the code completion tool, then type a pair of parentheses. Now, the first element from the enemyList array will be stored in the enemyImage variable.


Click ▶ to see the background color set to the first element of the backgroundColor array!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use setFlag to update the BounceOnWall property so that the Enemy sprites bounce when they hit the edges of the screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the for loop runs?

❓ What image will be used for the Enemy sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the for loop runs, 5 new Enemy sprites will be created and set to bounce on walls. The Enemy sprites’ image will be the first element in the enemyList array.

💡 Previously in JavaScript, the ninja has used the setBounceOnWalls function to code a sprite to bounce on walls. They can also use the setFlag function, which offers a list of many different sprite flags, to code a sprite to bounce on walls. This function uses the BounceOnWall property as a parameter.
steps.instructions:
Add multiple Enemy sprites to the project!


Open Loops and drag [for] under the existing code underneath // function set up. 


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the for loop’s curly brackets. Update the sprite name, use the enemyImage variable as the image parameter, and set the sprite kind as Enemy.


Open Sprites again and drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] underneath the Enemy sprite creation code. Update the sprite name, then change the flag parameter to BounceOnWall and the on parameter to true, so that the Enemy sprites bounce on walls. 


Click ▶ to see 5 Enemy sprites appear, set to the first image in the enemyList array!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you define a giveRandomPosition function with a Sprite parameter, and create 2 variables to set a sprite’s x and y-positions inside the function definition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might it be useful to create a function that sets a random position?

❓ What types of values can be used to set a function’s parameters?

❓ How are the randX and randY variables used in the setPosition code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Functions can be useful for defining a chunk of code that can be easily reused throughout a project. They also help organize the code in the editor by creating simple function calls within a chunk of code. 

💡 Point out to the ninja that when adding parameters to a function, the type must be defined. Parameters can accept number, string, sprite, image, or Boolean arguments. In this example, the sprite parameter will accept a Sprite argument, which will be used to assign a random position. 

💡 Remind the ninja that variables can be used in a function’s definition. This can be useful for changing the argument passed to a parameter throughout a project. In this example, different arguments will be passed to the function to set the sprite’s x and  y-positions, each time the function is called.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! All of the Enemy sprites appear on top of each other on the screen. 


Define a function to position the Enemy sprites randomly. Click Advanced then open Functions and drag [function doSomething] above the existing code underneath // function set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

function doSomething() {...} 

Rename the function giveRandomPosition then add a parameter to set which sprite should be positioned. Inside the function’s parentheses, type the parameter sprite and a colon : then set the type to Sprite 


Inside the function’s curly brackets, declare 2 new variables: randX and randY. Use randint to randomly assign each variable a value between 0 and the screen’s height or width. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x (x) y (y)] below the 2 variables. Replace mySprite with the sprite parameter from the function, then use randX and randY as the x and y parameters.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you call the giveRandomPosition function and pass the Enemy sprite’s name as an argument inside the parentheses?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where will Enemy sprites be placed on the screen when the giveRandomPosition function is called? 

❓ Why does the giveRandomPosition function need to be called inside the for loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that a function needs to be defined then called separately, in order for its code to run. 

💡 When the giveRandomPosition function is called, each Enemy sprite will be assigned a random position, determined by the randX and randY variables. This code needs to be placed within the for loop so that every Enemy sprite is assigned a random position, once created.
steps.instructions:
Call the function to set the position of the Enemy sprites.


Inside the for loop, call the giveRandomPosition function below the existing code. Type the function name and a pair of parentheses ( ) with the Enemy sprite’s name inside, to pass it as an argument to the function. The code might look like:

giveRandomPosition(enemy)

Click ▶ to see the project call the giveRandomPosition function each time a new Enemy sprite is created!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you define a giveRandomVelocity function, then call the function inside the for loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why are 2 different randX and randY variables able to be declared and used in the project?

❓ What will happen when the giveRandomVelocity function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that each function has its own set of curly brackets, which creates a block statement from the chunk of code within the function definition. As a result, the variables used within the function’s block statement are “scoped” to the function. That means that the code inside each function cannot be accessed by any other part of the project. This allows 2 different sets of the same variable names to be declared in 2 separate function definitions. 

💡 When the giveRandomVelocity function is called, the Enemy sprites will be assigned a random velocity determined by the randX and randY variables.
steps.instructions:
Use another function to assign each Enemy sprite a random velocity!


Create another function named giveRandomVelocity, then add a parameter to set which sprite should be given a random velocity. Inside the function’s parentheses, type the parameter sprite and a colon : then set the type to Sprite 


Inside the function’s curly brackets, declare new randX and randY variables. Use randint to set each variable to a random number between -30 and 30. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) velocity to vx (vx) vy (vy)] below the 2 variables. Replace mySprite with the sprite parameter from the function, then use randX and randY as the vx and vy parameters.


Inside the for loop, call the giveRandomVelocity function below the existing code. Type the function name and a pair of parentheses ( ) with the Enemy sprite’s name inside, to pass it as an argument to the function. The code might look like:

giveRandomVelocity(enemy) 

Click ▶ to see the project call the giveRandomVelocity function each time a new Enemy sprite is created!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use setFlag with the StayInScreen property so that the player doesn’t move off screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What image might you use for the Player sprite that would collect each image stored in the image variables?

❓ How is using the setFlag function to set a sprite to stay in screen different than using the setStayInScreen function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Previously in JavaScript, the ninja has used the setStayInScreen function to prevent a sprite from moving off screen. They can also use the setFlag function, which offers a list of many different sprite flags, to code a sprite to stay in screen. This function uses the StayInScreen function as a parameter.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // game set up. Select a Player sprite image and update the sprite name.


Allow the Player sprite to move around the screen. Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the sprite creation code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name.


Keep the Player sprite in screen. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] underneath Player sprite movement code. Update the sprite name, then change the flag parameter to SpriteFlag.StayInScreen and the on parameter to true.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite move around the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a destroy function with otherSprite inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event so that Enemy sprites disappear when they overlap with the Player sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite? What else might happen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite, the Enemy sprite will be destroyed. In the next step, the ninja will create a function that will set up each level. On overlap, this function will be called to create the next level.
steps.instructions:
Collect all the Enemy sprites!


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // game events. Leave the kind parameter as Player but change the otherKind parameter to Enemy. 


Open Sprites again and drag [destroy (mySprite)] inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event. Replace mySprite with otherSprite.


Click ▶ to see each Enemy sprite disappear on overlap with the Player sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you define a callLevel function with a number parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is the callLevel function used for? What will happen when it is called?

❓ What type of parameter can be passed to the callLevel function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The callLevel function is used to change the level in the project. On each level, different Enemy sprites will be created and a new background color will be set. It’s useful to add this code within a function so that it does not need to be typed multiple times in the project.

💡 The callLevel function can pass a number argument to the code, which will change the number and image of Enemy sprites and the background color, when it is called in the project.
steps.instructions:
Create a function to add new levels!


Define a function to call a new level. Click Advanced then open Functions and drag [function doSomething] underneath the existing code under // function set up. 


Rename the function callLevel then add a parameter to set the level number to be called. Inside the function’s parentheses, type the parameter level and a colon : then set the type to number


Cut (Ctrl + X) the setBackgroundColor, enemyImage, and for loop code and paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the curly brackets of the callLevel function definition. 


Now, each time the callLevel function is called, a new background color will be set and new Enemy sprites will be created.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the level function parameter inside the splash function, and as part of the run condition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What else will change each time a new level is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Now, when the callLevel function is called, the level number (updated by the level parameter) will be splashed on the screen, and an additional 5 Enemy sprites will be created on each subsequent level.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the function parameters can be used in the function’s definition code to further customize the code. The argument submitted in the function call will be passed into the function code.
steps.instructions:
Splash the level number on screen and increase the number of Enemy sprites when each level is called.


Open Game and drag [splash (title)] below the setBackgroundColor code inside the curly brackets of the callLevel function. Update the title parameter so that the string “level” is concatenated with the level function parameter.


Inside the for loop’s run condition, multiply 5 by the function’s parameter, so that the loop runs for a greater number of times as the level increases. The code might look like: 

i < 5 * level;

Now, each time the callLevel function is called, the level number will be splashed and a greater number of Enemy sprites will be created.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you call the callLevel function and pass the levelNum variable as the argument?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What level will the project be set to when it is started?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the project begins, Level 1 will be called, as that is the initial value of the levelNum variable. The variable will be increased in the next step, before the function is called so that the next level is used.

💡 Point out to the ninja that variables can be used to pass an argument to a function’s parameter. This can be useful for using different values as a function’s parameter throughout a project.
steps.instructions:
Call the first level at the beginning of the project!


Use a variable to set the level called. Underneath // game set up, use the keyword let to declare a new variable called levelNum and assign it a value of 1.


Call the callLevel function below the levelNum variable declaration. Type the function name and a pair of parentheses with levelNum inside, so that level 1 is called at the beginning of the project.


Click ▶ to call the callLevel function to start Level 1!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you increase the levelNum variable, then call the callLevel function inside the if conditional and pass the levelNum variable as the argument?
steps.instructions:
Call the next level once the Player sprite has collected all of the Enemy sprites!


Open Logic and drag [if] inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event, underneath the destroy code. 


Then, open Sprites and drag [array of sprites of kind (kind)] inside the parentheses of the conditional. Change the kind parameter to Enemy, then type a dot operator after allOfKind( ) and select length from the code completion tool. Use an equality operator to make something happen when there are 0 Enemy sprites on screen.


Increase the levelNum variable to change the next level called. Inside the conditional, use an increment operator ++ to increase the value of the levelNum by 1. The code should look like: 

levelNum++

Call the next level inside the conditional. Type the function name and a pair of parentheses ( ) with levelNum inside, to pass it as an argument to the function.


Click ▶ to see a new level called once all of the Enemy sprites have been collected from a level!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add an if else conditional inside the callLevel function definition and move all the existing code inside the curly brackets of the if condition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the level only change if there are images in the enemyList array? 

❓ What message might the be splashed on the screen to tell the user that all of the Enemy sprites have been collected?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the shift function is used to set the Enemy sprite’s image. This function returns and removes the first element in the enemyList array. As a result, if the length of the array is 0, then the user has moved through all 4 levels and has won the game.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the  setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
Allow the level to change only if there are still Enemy images left in the array!


Open Logic and drag [if else] inside of the callLevel function definition. Inside the parentheses of the conditional, add code to make something happen if the enemyList.length is greater than 0. Then, cut (Ctrl + X) the existing code inside the function and paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the if condition.


End the game once all of the Enemy sprite images have been used. Open Game and drag [splash (title)] inside the else condition. Update the title parameter with a string that tells the user that all of the Enemy sprites have been collected.


Open Game again and drag [game over (true)] below the splash code. Change the win parameter to true and add an effect parameter, too.


Click ▶ to see the game end once the Player sprite has collected all of the Enemy sprites in each level.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a countdown timer and customize its duration parameter as well as its border color?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How long might the countdown timer be set for so that the user has enough time to move through all of the levels?

❓ What color might be used as the border for the countdown timer?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the setBorderColor is another example of a function available in the “secret menu” in the JavaScript editor. 

💡 Remind the ninja that they should use a challenging, but not impossible amount of time in the countdown timer. This allows for difficult but fun game play in the project.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding directions and a countdown timer!


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] above the existing code underneath // game set up. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow.


Open Info and drag [start countdown (10) (s)] below the Player sprite’s code underneath // game set up. Update the duration parameter to set how long the Player sprite has to collect all of the Enemy sprites across all 4 levels. 


Set the countdown border color by accessing the info namespace. Below the startCountdown code, type info and a dot operator, then select setBorderColor from the code completion tool. Type a pair of parentheses with a number between 1-15 typed inside to set the countdown timer border color. Make sure that the border color will be visible in each of the project background colors!


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a multi-level project that uses functions to run code each time a level is changed.

validationItems.text: Store image variables in an enemyList array and background colors in a backgroundColor array.
Use the arrays and the shift function to set the background color and enemy sprite image.
Use a for loop to add multiple Enemy sprites and set them to bounce on walls.
Define a giveRandomPosition function to position the Enemy sprites randomly using randX and randY variables.
Call the giveRandomPosition function to set the position of the Enemy sprites.
Define a function to give the Enemy sprites random velocities and call it.
Add a Player sprite, move it with the controller, and set it to stay in screen.
When a Player sprite overlaps with an Enemy sprite, destroy the Enemy sprite.
Create a callLevel function with a level parameter to change the level and use the splash function to tell the user.
Create a levelNum variable to store the current level’s number, call the callLevel function with the current level, and increment the value of the levelNum variable.
When the user has collected all the Enemy sprites, call the callLevel function and increment the levelNum variable.
Allow the level to change only if there are still enemy images in the enemyList array. Use a splash screen to tell the user when they have collected all the enemies.
Add a countdown timer and change its border color.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about functions. Functions can be used to name a unique chunk of code that can be easily reused in a project. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: Function Junction
badges.description: Create and call functions that use different parameter types in JavaScript.

badges.title: Functional Thinking
badges.description: Create a new function, with or without parameters, in JavaScript.

badges.title: Calling All Functions
badges.description: Call a function, with or without parameters, in JavaScript.

badges.title: Time for a Change
badges.description: Change the border color of the countdown timer.

badges.title: Feeling Shifty
badges.description: Use the shift function to remove and return the first value in an array.

badges.title: Read the Manual
badges.description: Use a block comment to document a function.

badges.title: Free Fallin’
badges.description: Set the acceleration of a sprite to simulate gravity.
